query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a portion of the ferromagnetic element (Co) with an antiferromagnetic element (Cr) in an equiatomic FeCoNi high‐entropy alloy will induce local lattice distortions and minor phase heterogeneity that enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy, thereby increasing the alloy’s coercivity compared to the pure FeCoNi baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic FeCoNi high‐entropy alloy with a single fcc phase exhibiting high saturation magnetization and soft ferromagnetic behavior.
generation.intervention: Replace part of Co with Cr while preserving an equiatomic, high entropy composition (e.g. forming a FeCoNiCr alloy).
generation.conditions: The alloy must maintain near-equiatomic ratios and a high configurational entropy (≥1.0R) under processing conditions (such as controlled annealing) that promote controlled lattice distortion or a limited incipient phase transformation without excessive degradation of the primary fcc structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Cr-induced lattice distortions and nanoscale heterogeneity (or partial transition toward a lower-symmetry phase) that serve as effective domain wall pinning sites.
generation.mechanism: The antiferromagnetic nature of Cr interacts with the ferromagnetic Fe, Co, and Ni matrix to lower local symmetry and enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy. This facilitates increased domain wall pinning, thereby raising the coercivity of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The FeCoNiCr high-entropy alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly higher coercive field relative to the baseline FeCoNi alloy, although a modest reduction in saturation magnetization may occur.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy processed without Cr substitution, which is known to exhibit soft magnetic behavior with low coercivity.
generation.boundary: The coercivity enhancement is expected only when Cr substitution is optimized under controlled thermal treatments. Excessive Cr content or inappropriate annealing may lead to undesirable phase separations that could compromise the magnetic performance.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of coercivity increase and any trade-off with saturation magnetization depend on the exact Cr substitution level and processing parameters; these effects remain to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one set of the baseline equiatomic FeCoNi alloy and another with controlled substitution of Co by Cr (forming FeCoNiCr) while preserving equiatomic proportions. Process both sets under identical controlled annealing conditions to ensure comparable microstructural evolution. Use structural characterization (e.g., XRD and TEM) to verify that the intended phase(s) and microstructural features, such as lattice distortion or minor heterogeneity, are present exclusively in the Cr-substituted alloy. Subsequently, perform magnetic hysteresis measurements at room temperature to determine the coercive field and saturation magnetization of both alloys.
measurements: X-ray diffraction and TEM for phase identification and lattice distortion analysis
Magnetic hysteresis measurements (coercivity and saturation magnetization)
Chemical analysis (EDS or similar) to confirm elemental compositions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FeCoNiCr alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in coercivity compared to the baseline FeCoNi alloy, or if the Cr substitution leads to excessive secondary phase formation that adversely affects the magnetic properties (e.g., too large a decrease in saturation magnetization), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It should be noted that minor and well-dispersed Mn-Cr oxides with an average size of 8.94 μm were present in CoCrFeMnNi, as shown in Fig. 2. The composition of the Mn-Cr oxides is listed in Table 1. The presence Mn-Cr oxides in CoCrFeMnNi were previously reported by Tasan et al.. It appears that it is difficult to eliminate these Mn-Cr oxides in CoCrFeMnNi, and they might have hindered the migration of grain boundaries. Nevertheless, CoCrFeMnNi showed a homogeneous grain size distribution after one-step recrystallization (REC). The ratios of recrystallization temperature over melting temperature for CoCrFeMnNi, CoCrFeNi, and FeCoNi are 0.75, 0.63, and 0.57, respectively. These ratios increased with increasing alloying elements, which can be caused by severe lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion, which impede dislocation movement. Table 2 shows the REC results of CoCrFeMnNi, CoCrFeNi, and FeCoNi with varying grain size. Figures 3 and 4 show the remained strain analysis by misorientation distribution and the GBCD of the tested alloys, respectively.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Dislocation mechanisms for fcc to hcp phase transformation
cited_evidence.text: We have shown the existence of a nanostructure with hcp phase in the equiatomic CrCoNi—an alloy widely considered to have a single-phase fcc structure. We observed a delineation between CrCoNi—with hcp as the ground state independent of the local atomic arrangements—and the CrCoMnFeNi HEA, where the magnetic frustration resulting from the addition of Mn breaks a clear trend for relative hcp vs fcc energies. In addition, we showed that there is no driving force for this phase transformation in any other equiatomic ternary derivatives of this HEA. These findings emphasize the fact that high-entropy alloys with more constituent elements are not necessarily superior to their derivatives. Instead, the combination of chemical and, as emphasized presently, magnetic identities of elements govern the properties. An important consequence of this finding is that new alloying combinations can be predicted based on similar favorable magnetic properties. These results provide a new paradigm for design of single-phase alloys with metastable structures through computational guidance and experimental validation.

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small, controlled amount of interstitial carbon into an equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy will increase its coercivity compared to the previously studied Pd- or Pt-containing analogs.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic FeCoNi-based fcc high-entropy alloy with low coercivity and high saturation magnetization
drafts.intervention: Interstitial doping with a low concentration of carbon during alloy processing
drafts.conditions: The alloy must remain nearly equiatomic with a configurational entropy of at least 1.0R; carbon content should be kept below the solubility limit so as to induce controlled lattice distortions without forming carbide precipitates. The processing (e.g., annealing) should allow uniform carbon incorporation within the fcc matrix in a temperature range where the fcc phase is stable.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions/tetragonality induced by interstitial carbon atoms
drafts.mechanism: The interstitial carbon atoms create local strain fields that distort the fcc lattice toward slight tetragonality. This distortion enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy and increases the resistance to domain wall motion, thereby raising the coercivity of the alloy, even though the overall saturation magnetization remains high.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The alloy will exhibit a higher coercive field (i.e. it will be magnetically harder) than the soft ferromagnetic FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt derivatives, while maintaining a similar overall equiatomic configuration.
drafts.baseline: FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys with Pd or Pt, which have shown soft ferromagnetic behavior with low coercivity
drafts.boundary: This effect is expected to be observable when the carbon content is optimized to produce significant lattice distortions without inducing secondary carbide phases. Extremely high carbon levels or processing conditions that lead to phase separation could negate the desired coercivity enhancement.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of equiatomic FeCoNi alloys with incremental interstitial carbon additions (e.g., 0, 1, 2, and 3 at.% carbon) under identical processing conditions. Characterize their crystal structures using XRD and TEM to confirm the degree of lattice distortion and phase purity. Measure magnetic hysteresis loops to extract coercivity values at room temperature.
measurements: Lattice parameters and phase analysis (via XRD, TEM)
Carbon distribution (via EDS or atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloys do not show a statistically significant increase in coercivity compared to the baseline FeCoNi alloy (or if secondary carbide phases form at the targeted carbon levels), the hypothesis that controlled interstitial carbon doping increases coercivity would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing interstitial nitrogen into an equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy will induce local lattice distortions that enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy and lead to increased coercivity relative to the undoped alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: An almost equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy (e.g., FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt) exhibiting a single-phase fcc structure with high saturation magnetization but soft ferromagnetic behavior (i.e., low coercivity)
drafts.intervention: Perform a controlled nitriding treatment (i.e., interstitial nitrogen doping) on the alloy to incorporate a modest amount of nitrogen into the lattice
drafts.conditions: The nitriding should be executed at moderate temperatures that allow nitrogen diffusion without causing phase separation or significant deviations from the fcc structure, thereby retaining the high configurational entropy (≥1.0R) of the alloy
drafts.structural_mediator: Interstitial nitrogen atoms introduce local lattice distortions; these distortions can break the cubic symmetry locally (or induce a minor tetragonal distortion) that enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy and creates effective domain wall pinning sites
drafts.mechanism: Nitrogen incorporation occupies interstitial sites within the fcc lattice, causing local strain and altering the electronic and crystallographic environment. This increases the crystal anisotropy energy, which is expected to contribute to a higher coercivity by impeding domain wall motion
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped baseline FeCoNiPd (or FeCoNiPt) alloy, the nitrided alloy will exhibit a measurable increase in coercivity while retaining high saturation magnetization and single-phase character
drafts.baseline: Equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy (such as FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt) processed without nitriding, which is known to exhibit soft ferromagnetism
drafts.boundary: This intervention is predicted to be effective when the nitriding conditions (temperature and nitrogen partial pressure) are optimized such that nitrogen is uniformly incorporated without triggering secondary phase formation or undesired phase transformations

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to a controlled nitriding treatment under optimized conditions, while keeping a second set as the untreated baseline. Characterize both sets via X-ray diffraction (to ensure retention of the fcc phase and detect any lattice distortions), measure nitrogen uptake (using techniques such as SIMS or EDS), and perform magnetic hysteresis measurements to determine coercivity and saturation magnetization.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification and detection of lattice distortions
Nitrogen concentration analysis (SIMS, EDS, or XPS)
Magnetic hysteresis loops (to extract coercivity, Hc, and saturation magnetization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrided samples do not show a statistically significant increase in coercivity (relative to the undoped baseline) or if the nitriding process induces phase separation or loss of the desired fcc structure, the hypothesis is falsified

drafts.hypothesis: Replacing part of the ferromagnetic element (Co) with an antiferromagnetic element (Cr) in an equiatomic FeCoNi-based high‐entropy alloy will promote nanoscale phase heterogeneity and low‐symmetry ordering that enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy and increases coercivity compared to the previously reported soft FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single-phase face‐centered cubic (fcc) FeCoNi alloy with high saturation magnetization and low coercivity
drafts.intervention: Substitute a portion of Co with Cr so that the resulting composition is still equiatomic (e.g., Fe, Co, Ni, Cr, plus one balancing element if needed to reach ≥5 principal elements and ΔSmix ≥1.0R)
drafts.conditions: The alloy should be processed (e.g., via controlled annealing) under conditions that do not fully homogenize the microstructure, thus encouraging nanoscale phase separation or formation of low‐symmetry chemical ordering; temperature windows where partial phase decomposition can occur (e.g., moderate annealing temperatures) are preferred.
drafts.structural_mediator: The introduction of Cr is expected to induce the formation of antiferromagnetically aligned regions or Cr‐rich nano‐domains and lower the overall symmetry (e.g., promoting a local transition or incipient ordering toward a tetragonal/L10 or mixed-phase arrangement), which act as effective pinning centers for domain walls.
drafts.mechanism: Cr, being antiferromagnetic, will interact with the ferromagnetic Fe, Co, and Ni matrix to create local variations in exchange interactions. These, in concert with possible strain and chemical inhomogeneity, lead to increased magnetocrystalline anisotropy and enhanced domain wall pinning. This structural and magnetic heterogeneity increases the intrinsic coercivity relative to the soft ferromagnets produced with Pd or Pt additions that tend to preserve high-symmetry fcc ordering.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Cr-substituted equiatomic high-entropy alloy is expected to show a markedly increased coercive field compared to FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt derivatives, with a likely (but acceptable) trade-off of a reduced saturation magnetization.
drafts.baseline: FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys having near-equiatomic compositions that do not include Cr (such as previously studied FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt systems) which exhibit soft magnetic behavior (low coercivity)
drafts.boundary: This effect is expected when the overall processing preserves high configurational entropy (≥1.0R) and when the annealing conditions favor partial ordering or phase separation; excessive thermal homogenization might remove the nanoscale heterogeneity necessary for the coercivity enhancement.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of equiatomic high-entropy alloy samples: one based on the baseline FeCoNi (or a known soft derivative such as FeCoNiPd/Pt) and one where a predetermined fraction of Co is replaced by Cr to yield an equiatomic 5-element or 4-element composition. Process both sets under identical annealing conditions optimized to allow incipient phase separation. Characterize the crystal structure (using XRD and TEM) to confirm the retention of high configurational entropy and the presence of nanoscale heterogeneity. Subsequently, measure the magnetic hysteresis loops (using vibrating sample magnetometry or SQUID magnetometry) to extract coercivity (Hc) and saturation magnetization (Ms).
measurements: Phase identification and microstructural features (XRD, TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-substituted high-entropy alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in coercive field compared to the baseline sample, or if detailed microstructural characterization reveals no evidence of the anticipated low-symmetry ordering or nanoscale phase heterogeneity, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Replacing a portion of the FeCoNi alloy with chromium to form an equiatomic FeCoNiCr high-entropy alloy will promote a partial fcc-to-hcp transformation and/or enhanced lattice distortion that increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy, thereby increasing the coercivity compared to the pure FeCoNi baseline.
drafts.material_initial_state: An equiatomic, single-phase FeCoNi high-entropy alloy with an fcc structure, high saturation magnetization, and low coercivity.
drafts.intervention: Introduce chromium as a fourth equiatomic element (i.e. synthesize FeCoNiCr) while maintaining nearly equiatomic proportions to preserve high configurational entropy (≥1.0R).
drafts.conditions: The alloy must be processed under conditions (e.g., controlled annealing/thermal treatment) that support the coexistence of an fcc matrix and a controlled amount of a secondary, lower-symmetry (hcp) phase. The processing conditions should allow for lattice distortion without excessive loss of saturation magnetization.
drafts.structural_mediator: The inclusion of Cr is expected to induce lattice frustration, lowering the overall symmetry through a partial phase transformation (fcc to hcp) and increasing the density of defects and grain boundaries that serve as pinning sites.
drafts.mechanism: Chromium has an antiferromagnetic tendency and can promote magnetic frustration when added to ferromagnetic systems. Its inclusion is anticipated to facilitate a controlled fcc-to-hcp transformation (or the development of a dual-phase microstructure) that increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy. This, in turn, enhances domain wall pinning, resulting in an increased coercivity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The engineered FeCoNiCr alloy will exhibit a significantly higher coercivity compared to the baseline FeCoNi alloy, while retaining a moderately high saturation magnetization.
drafts.baseline: The pure equiatomic FeCoNi alloy, which crystallizes in a high-symmetry fcc structure and exhibits soft ferromagnetic behavior (i.e., low coercivity).
drafts.boundary: This effect is expected to hold under processing conditions that allow for controlled phase formation. Excessive Cr addition or unsuitable thermal treatment may destabilize the desired microstructure or reduce the saturation magnetization beyond acceptable limits.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two high-entropy alloys: (1) the baseline equiatomic FeCoNi alloy and (2) the equiatomic FeCoNiCr alloy. Process both samples identically using controlled annealing conditions to ensure comparable microstructural evolution. Perform structural characterization using X-ray diffraction to detect any fcc-to-hcp transformation and measure the magnetic hysteresis loops using vibrating sample magnetometry.
measurements: Phase constitution and lattice symmetry via X-ray diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FeCoNiCr alloy does not exhibit a significant increase in coercivity (e.g., more than a 20% improvement relative to the FeCoNi baseline) while maintaining acceptable saturation magnetization, then the hypothesis is falsified.
